question: Back in \(1930,\) Tillie had to memorize her multiplication facts from \(0 \times 0\) through \(12 \times 12.\) The multiplication table she was given had rows and columns labeled with the factors, and the products formed the body of the table. To the nearest hundredth, what fraction of the numbers in the body of the table are odd?
solution:
A product is odd exactly when both factors are odd. Thus we can count the relevant row and column labels without computing the entire table.

The labels run from \(0\) through \(12\), inclusive, so there are \(13\) rows and \(13\) columns. Each row-column pair specifies one cell, giving
\[
13\cdot13=169
\]
entries in the body. Equal products appearing in different cells are still separate entries.

The odd labels are \(1,3,5,7,9,11\), giving six choices for each factor. Each of the six odd-labeled rows has an odd product in exactly the six odd-labeled columns. Hence there are \(6\cdot6=36\) odd entries, counted once each by their cell positions.

The requested fraction is
\[
\frac{36}{169}\approx0.2130,
\]
which rounds to \(\boxed{0.21}\) to the nearest hundredth, choice A.
